subject: economics
title: Expectations and NAIRU
welcome_lead: Long run, the curve is vertical at the natural rate.
meta_desc: A-Level Phillips Curve: expectations-augmented and long-run vertical curve.
final_note: Once expectations adjust, the trade-off disappears.

concepts.def: Combination of high inflation and unemployment.

walkthroughs.body_html: In 1968, Friedman argued workers eventually anticipate inflation and demand higher wages. The short-run gain in employment vanishes - only inflation persists.
The long-run Phillips curve sits vertical at NAIRU. Any attempt to push unemployment below NAIRU produces only accelerating inflation.
The 1970s oil shocks brought stagflation - high inflation and high unemployment. The original Phillips curve could not explain it; the expectations-augmented version could.

mcqs.q: In the long run the Phillips curve is:
Friedman argued the short-run trade-off vanishes because:
options: Workers anticipate inflation and demand higher wages

mcqs.q: What did the original Phillips curve suggest, and how has thinking changed?
options: Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.
The Phillips curve still proves you can always reduce unemployment by allowing more inflation.

The original Phillips curve suggested a stable inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Friedman and the 1970s stagflation experience added expectations — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

mcqs.q: How does raising interest rates reduce inflation?
options: Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
Higher interest rates directly force shops to lower their prices.
Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reducing consumption and investment — lowering aggregate demand and slowing price rises.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
Inflation is when prices are high.
A sustained rise in the general price level over time — reducing the purchasing power of money. Measured by the percentage change in a price index.
Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
